value.overview: The Cinnamon Woodpecker (Celeus loricatus) is a medium-sized woodpecker of humid tropical forests in Central and northern South America. Its mostly cinnamon-brown plumage, shaggy crest, dark bill, and pale facial markings give it a distinctive appearance. It is generally uncommon and can be difficult to see because it often forages quietly in dense vegetation or high in the canopy. Costa Rica lies near the northern part of its range.
value.classification: The Cinnamon Woodpecker belongs to the woodpecker family Picidae and the genus Celeus. It is classified in the order Piciformes.
value.identification: This woodpecker is about 19–20 cm long and has predominantly cinnamon or warm rufous-brown plumage, a long shaggy crest, and a fairly dark, chisel-shaped bill. The underparts may appear somewhat paler or more barred depending on subspecies and lighting. It is often recognized by its distinctive loud, far-carrying call, described as a repeated wheeét-like phrase. Sexes are similar overall, although males may show a small contrasting mark near the bill or cheek.
value.rangeHabitat: The Cinnamon Woodpecker occurs from Costa Rica and Nicaragua through Panama to Colombia, western Ecuador, and parts of the Magdalena region. In Costa Rica it is a native resident of lowland and foothill areas, generally below about 800 m, and is associated especially with humid to wet evergreen forest. It may also use forest edges, secondary woodland, clearings, and well-treed pastures, but it is most closely linked to landscapes retaining mature forest structure.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; no regular long-distance migration is known.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding activity has been reported mainly from March through May. Both members of a pair excavate a nest cavity, usually in a living or recently dead tree. The cavity is generally placed several metres above the ground. Available information on clutch size, incubation, nestling development, and division of parental care remains limited, so the species’ complete breeding biology is not well documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Cinnamon Woodpecker feeds mainly on ants and termites, which it obtains by pecking into bark, wood, and decaying branches or by gleaning from surfaces. It may also take fruit, including cultivated or soft fruits when available. In forest interiors it commonly forages in the middle and upper levels of trees, while in more open habitats it may search lower on trunks and branches. It is usually seen alone or in pairs.
value.behavior: This species is generally unobtrusive and is often detected by its voice before it is seen. It forages methodically on trunks, limbs, and dead wood, sometimes joining mixed-species feeding flocks. Its flight is typically undulating, as in many woodpeckers. The Cinnamon Woodpecker uses short, relatively slow drumming and several calls, including loud repeated notes and sharper chattering sounds when disturbed or agitated.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although it remains large enough and widespread enough for the species to remain classified as Least Concern.
